newsitem.title: INDIA: Regional parties are kingmakers in India.
newsitem.headline: Regional parties are kingmakers in India.

text.p: India's regional political parties, products of the nation's growing economic and political federalism, hold the key to the formation of a new coalition government, politicians and analysts said on Wednesday.

The regional parties -- two from Tamil Nadu state, one from Andhra Pradesh and the fourth from Assam -- have emerged as important power brokers within caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 15-party United Front coalition.
"The rise of regional parties has emerged as an important factor in national politics," V.A. Pai Panandikar, director of the Centre for Policy Research (CPR), told Reuters.

The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), Telegu Desam Party (TDP), Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) and Asom Gana Parishad (AGP) joined hands last year to form the Federal Front bloc, which later was folded into the United Front.
The four parties have 59 of the United Front's 178 deputies in the 542-member parliament. Deve Gowda's Janata Dal party is the coalition's biggest single party with 45 deputies.
Federal Front leaders on Sunday prevailed upon the United Front leadership to elect a new leader to replace Deve Gowda.

The Congress party, which triggered a political crisis by withdrawing support from the United Front on March 30, had demanded that Deve Gowda be removed before extending fresh support to a new ruling coalition.
The regional parties saw their clout in the federal parliament grow dramatically in last year's general elections, and they are reluctant to go back to the polls.
They are now expected to be kingmakers, and may even see one of their own coronated. TMC leader G.K. Moopanar was considered a frontrunner in the jockeying to be the next prime minister.
The parties reflect growing federalism in a nation of 936 million people and dozens of languages.

"The regional parties reflect the aspirations of the people at the local level. It also shows the communication gap of the national parties with their state organisations," senior Congress leader Ved Prakash told Reuters.

In 1951, India adopted centralised planning under its first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, to boost economic growth. The socialist model failed to deliver desired results at the state level, Panandikar said.
"Economic federalism largely arose out of the failure of socialist and centralised planning methods," he said.
The regional parties filled a void left by national parties and articulated the demands of the people in different states.
They have asked for greater economic autonomy and a shift of power from the central government to the states.

Currently, India's 26 states have limited means of raising finances, as tax revenues from income, excise and import tariffs are collected by the federal government. The states earn revenues from sales and other local taxes.
After India launched a sweeping economic reform programme in 1991, most states introduced liberal policies to woo investors.
Most investment decisions are now taken by states, and that trend is seen as increasing no matter who rules in New Delhi.
"There has also been a transfer of power from upper castes to backward and lower castes," said Panandikar.
The rise of lower caste Bahujan Samaj Party in India's most populous Uttar Pradesh state reflects the transfer.
The BSP's Mayawati (Eds: one name) was named chief of Uttar Pradesh state last month with the support of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
